meta.title: System Design Roadmap for Beginners | Parmeshwar Metkar posted on the topic | LinkedIn
meta.description:
🚀 Want to learn System Design but don’t know where to start?

Don’t jump straight into designing WhatsApp, Zomato, or Netflix.

First, build the foundation. 🧠

Here’s a practical System Design Roadmap:

🔹 Phase 1 — Networking Basics
• How the Internet works
• TCP vs UDP
• HTTP/HTTPS & TLS
• DNS Resolution
• REST APIs

🔹 Phase 2 — Core Building Blocks
• Load Balancers
• CDN
• Redis & Caching
• API Gateway
• SQL vs NoSQL
• Kafka & Message Queues

🔹 Phase 3 — Patterns & Concepts
• CAP Theorem
• Consistent Hashing
• Database Sharding
• Idempotency
• Outbox Pattern
• Saga & CQRS
• Rate Limiting

🔹 Phase 4 — Real-World Design
• URL Shortener
• Chat System
• Food Delivery App
• Notification System
• Rate Limiter

💡 The biggest mistake?
Trying to solve complex system-design problems before understanding the fundamentals.

Build the foundation → Learn the building blocks → Understand the patterns → Design real systems.

Save this roadmap 📌 and use it as your System Design learning checklist.

⏱️ Latency — time for one request to make a round trip
📊 Throughput — how many requests get handled per second
📶 Bandwidth — the max data capacity of the link itself
📈 Jitter — how consistent that delay actually is, request to request

Most setups look fine on paper until jitter spikes under real traffic — that's usually where things quietly fall apart.

Which one do you check first when an API feels "slow"?

meta.title: Proxy vs Reverse Proxy vs VPN: What's the Difference? | Aman Mishra posted on the topic | LinkedIn
meta.description:
Proxy. Reverse proxy. VPN.
Most developers use all three every week.

Ask them the difference, and the answer gets vague fast.
One question clears it up: who is hiding whom?

(Day 13/30 — System Design for Beginners)

1️⃣ 𝗙𝗼𝗿𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗱 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘅𝘆 → 𝗵𝗶𝗱𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗟𝗜𝗘𝗡𝗧
You → Proxy → Website
The website sees the proxy's IP, not yours.
Think: you send a friend to buy something for you.
The shop only ever sees your friend.
Used for:
→ Office networks filtering which sites you can open
→ Hiding your IP
→ Caching common downloads for a whole office
It works on behalf of the client.

2️⃣ 𝗥𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘅𝘆 → 𝗵𝗶𝗱𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗘𝗥𝗩𝗘𝗥𝗦
Users → Reverse proxy (e.g. Nginx) → Server 1, Server 2
Users never see, or reach, your real servers.
Think: a company's reception desk.
You never get the employees' direct numbers.

Used for:
→ Load balancing
→ SSL termination (handle HTTPS once, at the edge)
→ Caching and compression
→ Blocking bad traffic before it reaches your app

It works on behalf of the server.
Here's the part that connects the series:
The load balancer (Day 8) and the API gateway (Day 12) are both reverse proxies.
Specialised ones, but the same idea.

3️⃣ 𝗩𝗣𝗡 → 𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗲𝘀 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗪𝗛𝗢𝗟𝗘 𝗗𝗘𝗩𝗜𝗖𝗘
Laptop ══ encrypted tunnel ══ Office network
Your device behaves as if it's inside that network.

The difference from a proxy:
→ A proxy usually handles one app's traffic, like your browser
→ A VPN works at the network level, so all your device's traffic goes through it, encrypted

Used for: reaching internal dashboards, databases, and tools from home.

🎯 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄 𝗮𝗻𝘀𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝗻 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲
"A forward proxy acts for the client, a reverse proxy acts for the server, and a VPN extends a private network to your device."
Say that, then give one example of each. Done.

𝗧𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆
→ Forward proxy hides the client.
→ Reverse proxy hides the servers.
→ VPN moves your whole device into another network.

Tomorrow, Day 14: recap of week 2. From 1 server to 1 million users, in one picture.
Which of these three did you mix up the longest?

👉 Follow Aman Mishra for more backend insights,content, and interview-focused tech breakdowns!🚀

𝗜𝗳 𝘆𝗼𝘂'𝗿𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸𝗲𝗻𝗱 𝗼𝗿 𝗦𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺 𝗗𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄𝘀, 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗶𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘆𝗼𝘂.

🚀 Spring Boot Interview Questions (Part 1)
After sharing Core Java & Java 8 questions, here are Spring Boot questions that were frequently asked in my interviews 👇
🔹 Core Spring Concepts
Explain Bean Lifecycle
What is Bean Scope? What is the default scope?
🔹 Scope-Based Scenario
If a class has singleton scope and it has a reference of prototype bean, how does it behave?
@Scope("singleton")
class A {
    B b;
}

@Scope("prototype")
class B {
}
👉 Follow-up:
How can we ensure it behaves like prototype instead of singleton?
🔹 Important Comparisons
Java Singleton vs Spring Singleton Scope
Difference between @Primary and @Qualifier
🔹 Transaction Management
Transactions, Propagation, and Isolation
👉 Scenario-based questions on propagation
🔹 Annotations & Config
What annotations have you used? Explain them
@RequestBody is used for JSON → Java object
👉 What if you want to support another data format?
@ConfigurationProperties vs @Value
@ConditionalOnProperty
How to create beans based on environment or condition
🔹 Spring Security
Spring Security basics
JWT
Authentication vs Authorization
🔹 Web Layer
@PathVariable vs @RequestParam
🔹 Build Tool
Maven Lifecycle
🔹 Spring Data JPA
What is @Repository?
interface StudentRepo extends JpaRepository<Student, Integer> {
}
👉 Why Integer is used instead of int?
🔹 Configuration Files
If same values are defined in both .properties and .yml, which one is loaded first?
🔹 Database
How to use multiple databases in a single Spring Boot application?
🔹 APIs
What are Spring Boot Starters?
SOAP API vs REST API
Advantages and disadvantages of REST API
Difference between @RestController and @Controller
🔹 Dependency Injection
What is Dependency Injection?
Types of Dependency Injection
Which one do you prefer and why?
🔹 Profiles & AOP
Profiles in Spring Boot
Spring AOP
Filter vs Interceptor
🔹 Miscellaneous
How to upload file and save in DB
@Async vs CompletableFuture

meta.title: Infosys Java Spring Boot Microservices Interview Experience | Er. Naimuddin Alam posted on the topic | LinkedIn
meta.description:
🚀 Infosys Interview Experience | Java | Spring Boot | Microservices | Kafka
I recently attended an interview with Infosys for a Senior Java / Spring Boot / Microservices role.
The interview was mainly focused on real-world scenarios, scalability, performance, fault tolerance, distributed systems, and system design rather than only theoretical concepts.
🔹 Questions Asked
Java / Design Principles
Explain SOLID principles with real-world examples.
Spring Boot / Hibernate
What is the N+1 problem in Hibernate?
How do you identify and resolve the N+1 problem?
How would you handle 5 lakh records efficiently?
How would you optimize a slow API?
Kafka
What is a Kafka Topic?
How does Kafka handle high-volume data?
What are partitions and consumer groups?
How do you handle failed Kafka messages?
Microservices / System Design
How would you design Payment, Inventory, and Notification services?
What happens if the Payment Service goes down?
What happens if Payment succeeds but Inventory Service fails?
What happens if the Notification Service is unavailable?
How do you handle distributed transactions?
What is the Saga Pattern?
What is a Circuit Breaker?
How would you handle retries and timeouts between microservices?
How do you implement Idempotency in payment processing?
SQL Server
What is a Stored Procedure?
Why would you use a Stored Procedure?
How would you optimize SQL queries for a large dataset?
CI/CD
What is CI/CD?
Explain a CI/CD pipeline for a Spring Boot application.
What happens if unit tests fail during the pipeline?
How would you handle a failed production deployment?
Docker
How do you Dockerize a Spring Boot application?
What is a Dockerfile?
What is the difference between a Docker image and a container?
How would you configure Spring Boot services using Docker Compose?
💡 Key Takeaway
The interview was not limited to theoretical questions. The interviewer focused heavily on how we would handle real production scenarios, especially:
🔹 Scalability → 5 lakh records
🔹 Performance → N+1 / Indexing / Pagination / Caching
🔹 Messaging → Kafka / Topics / Partitions / Consumer Groups
🔹 Reliability → Retry / Circuit Breaker / Idempotency
🔹 Distributed Transactions → Saga / Compensation
🔹 Database → Stored Procedures / Query Optimization
🔹 DevOps → Docker / CI/CD / Deployment
Overall, it was a good experience and a strong reminder that real-world problem solving and system design are just as important as knowing the technology itself.
👉 What questions were asked in your recent Infosys Java/Spring Boot/Microservices interview?
Please share your experience in the comments. It may help other developers prepare better for their interviews.

meta.description:
Company name : Honey Bee 
Java Full Stack Interview Questions

Sharing some of the Java, Spring Boot, Microservices, and Angular interview questions discussed during my interview experience at Honey Bee, Viman Nagar.

🏗️ Microservices

1. What are the ways to communicate between services?
    * How can two microservices communicate with each other?
    * REST API vs asynchronous communication such as messaging.

🅰️ Angular

2. What is the lifecycle of Angular hooks?
    * Explain lifecycle hooks such as ngOnInit, ngOnChanges, ngDoCheck, ngAfterViewInit, and ngOnDestroy.
3. What is the structure of an Angular component?
    * Component
    * Template
    * Class
    * Metadata/decorators
    * Styles
4. What are Directives in Angular?
    * Structural directives
    * Attribute directives
    * Examples such as *ngIf, *ngFor, and ngClass.

☕ Java 8

5. How do you calculate the frequency of elements in a list using Java 8?

6. What is return in Java?
    * What is the purpose of the return statement?
    * Difference between returning a value and using return; in a void method.

🌱 Spring / Spring Boot

7. What are the different Bean Scopes in Spring?
    * Singleton
    * Prototype
    * Request
    * Session
    * Application
    * WebSocket
8. What is Prototype Scope?
    * How is it different from Singleton?
    * When would you use prototype-scoped beans?
9. ApplicationContext vs BeanFactory
    * What is ApplicationContext?
    * What is BeanFactory?
    * What are their differences and use cases?

📁 Files

10. Custom files vs normal files

* What is meant by custom file handling?
* How are custom files different from normal/static files?
* How would you handle them in an application?

💡 Interview Takeaway

The discussion covered a combination of Microservices communication, Angular, Java 8 Streams, Spring Bean Scopes, Spring IoC containers, and file handling.

These questions are a good reminder that Java Full Stack interviews can cover multiple layers of an application—from frontend component lifecycle to backend service communication and Spring’s dependency management.

Sharing these questions to help fellow developers preparing for their upcoming Java Full Stack / Spring Boot / Microservices interviews. 🚀

meta.title: #systemdesign #softwareengineering #ratelimiting #distributedsystems #backenddevelopment #nodejs #redis #apidesign | Jakshi Jindal
meta.description:
𝗢𝗻𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗔𝗣𝗜 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺𝘀 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗮 𝘀𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺.
While working with APIs, I started thinking about what happens when one client sends far more requests than expected.
For example:
𝗡𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗹 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰
Client → API → Server → DB
𝗨𝗻𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰
Client → → → → → → API → Server → DB 💥

The interesting part is that the API might still be working correctly.
The problem is that one client can consume resources that should be shared by everyone.
That made me look at 𝗥𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗟𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴.
For example:
`100 requests / minute / client`
Requests 1–100 → ✅
Request 101 → ❌ `429 Too Many Requests`

But then I came across another problem.
What if the API has multiple instances?
𝗦𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝟭 → 30 requests
𝗦𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝟮 → 30 requests
𝗦𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝟯 → 30 requests
If every server maintains its own counter, the client could effectively make 90 requests even though we intended to enforce a shared limit.
So the counter needs to be shared across instances.
𝗦𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝟭 ─┐
𝗦𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝟮 ─┼→ 𝗥𝗲𝗱𝗶𝘀 → 𝗥𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗟𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘁
𝗦𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝟯 ─┘
And that's where the design becomes more interesting.

There are also different strategies like:
→ Fixed Window
→ Sliding Window
→ Token Bucket
→ Leaky Bucket

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗜 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗱 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴:
A problem that initially looks like “just count requests” becomes a distributed-systems problem once the API scales horizontally.

meta.title: Java Evolution: From 8 to 25 and Beyond | Nadeem Ahmad posted on the topic | LinkedIn
meta.description:
𝗝𝗮𝘃𝗮 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗱 𝗮 𝗹𝗼𝘁 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗹𝗮𝘀𝘁 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗮𝗱𝗲.

From Java 8 to Java 25, each LTS release has introduced important improvements that have shaped modern Java development.

Java 8 → Foundation
Java 11 → Modernization
Java 17 → Modern Java
Java 21 → Next-generation Java
Java 25 → Latest LTS

And while 𝗝𝗮𝘃𝗮 𝟮𝟲 𝗶𝘀 𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗹𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗝𝗮𝘃𝗮 𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗲, Java 25 remains the latest 𝗟𝗧𝗦 version.

If you're a Java developer, understanding this evolution helps you decide 𝘄𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗵 𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗼 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻, 𝗺𝗶𝗴𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝘁𝗼, 𝗼𝗿 𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝗶𝗻 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻.

𝗪𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗵 𝗝𝗮𝘃𝗮 𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗹𝘆 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵? 👇
